A MAJOR LEGAL MILESTONE IN THE PROTECTION OF ORCAS. 🐋

California's Orca Protection Act, enacted in 2016, made it illegal to breed or impregnate captive orcas in the state. It also prohibits keeping orcas for display, performance, or entertainment, with an exception for orcas already held in captivity before January 1, 2017.

Those existing orcas may continue to be held and used in qualifying educational presentations, but breeding is prohibited.

Anyone who intentionally or negligently violates the law can face misdemeanor charges and a fine of up to $100,000.

The law does not immediately release captive orcas, but it prevents future breeding and establishes important restrictions on their captivity.

Source: California Fish and Game Code, Section 4502.5 — California Orca Protection Act.

A CLOSE ENCOUNTER THAT REVEALED THE HIDDEN DANGERS OF OCEAN POLLUTION. 🐋

In 2024, wildlife guide Lorien Cleavinger encountered a female sperm whale in the Indian Ocean with floating trash and plant debris caught in its mouth and throat.

While other swimmers filmed, Cleavinger carefully removed pieces of debris with her bare hands. According to her account, the whale remained relatively still throughout the encounter and stayed near the group afterward.

Although the encounter had a positive outcome, approaching or touching wild whales is extremely dangerous for both people and animals. This remarkable moment also reminds us how marine pollution can affect even the ocean's largest creatures.

Source: DIVE Magazine, June 13, 2024; Lorien Cleavinger's account.

A REMARKABLE NEW CHAPTER IN AN ORCA FAMILY'S HISTORY. 🐋

In March 2025, researchers documented a new Bigg’s killer whale calf, T046B3A, in the Salish Sea. The calf belongs to a family descended from the Budd Inlet Six, a group of orcas captured in Washington in 1976.

Public pressure helped secure the release of six whales, with Ralph Munro among those who fought for their freedom. One female, later named Wake, was not released and remained in captivity.

In an extraordinary coincidence, Munro died on March 20, 2025—the same day the calf's arrival was announced. The young whale represents the continuation of a family line that survived a defining moment in orca conservation history.

Source: Smithsonian Magazine

The real story: On October 7, 2026, two juvenile humpback whales were found stuck on sandbars off Fire Island, New York. The U.S. Coast Guard helped respond, and both whales returned to open water as the tide rose. Source: ABC7 New York and News 12 Long Island, published October 8, 2026.

Two young humpback whales ran into trouble off Fire Island, New York, on October 7, 2026: both had become stuck on sandbars, in water too shallow to swim in. A stranded whale is in a race against the tide, because its body isn't built to be out of the water's support, and every hour on the sand increases the risk.

The U.S. Coast Guard responded to help rescue the juvenile humpbacks, and crews monitored both animals as the water began to rise. Local reports described the outcome as a happy one: the tide came in, the whales were freed, and both swam back out to sea.

It was a rare piece of good news in a season that has brought several whale strandings to the Northeast. The most important part of such a rescue, according to marine mammal responders, is what the public does and doesn't do: call the Coast Guard or a stranding network right away, stay back, and let trained responders decide whether to help or to let the tide do the work.

In 1976, a group of orcas was captured in Budd Inlet, near Olympia, Washington, in what became the last orca capture in United States waters. The public outcry was enormous. One of the people who fought hardest for their release was Ralph Munro, who later became Washington's secretary of state. Six whales were freed, but one of them, a female later named Wake, was taken to SeaWorld.

On March 20, 2025, researchers announced that a new Bigg's killer whale calf, catalogued T046B3A, had been spotted in the Salish Sea. It is a descendant of the Budd Inlet Six, the orcas Munro had helped rescue. The calf's mother is a member of the family that the 1976 captures nearly cut off. Munro's efforts, it turns out, are part of why those lines still exist.

The timing was uncanny. Ralph Munro died that same day, March 20, 2025, at age 81. The news of the calf and the news of his death arrived together. For the whale community, the story became a neat circle: a man who spent a part of his life fighting for orcas, and a new orca, born into a family he helped keep alive, on the day he passed.

A RESCUE EFFORT ENDED IN HEARTBREAK AFTER A YOUNG ORCA'S CONDITION BECAME IRREVERSIBLE.

On April 27, 2026, a juvenile male killer whale measuring approximately 4.28 metres was found stranded at Playa Mansa in Punta del Este, Uruguay.

Veterinarians and rescue teams made several attempts to stabilize him and return him to the ocean. However, his condition continued to deteriorate, and specialists ultimately decided to perform euthanasia to prevent further suffering.

A later necropsy revealed severe inflammation and infection in his brain, along with advanced pneumonia. Researchers identified neurobrucellosis as the likely underlying cause of the stranding.

Although the rescue could not save him, the examination provided valuable information about the health challenges facing wild marine mammals.

Sources: University of the Republic of Uruguay, May 2026; El País, May 12, 2026.

74 years ago today, one American pilot took on seven Soviet MiGs… alone. 

November 18, 1952.
Navy Lieutenant Royce Williams was flying an F9F Panther off the coast of Korea when he suddenly found himself facing seven Soviet MiG-15s.

Outnumbered.
Outmatched in speed and climb.
And completely alone.

For 35 minutes — the longest dogfight in U.S. Navy history — Williams fought them.
He shot down four of the Soviet jets.
His plane was hit by a 37mm cannon shell, hydraulics failing, yet he still made it back to the carrier and landed.

Because the enemy pilots were Soviet (not North Korean or Chinese), the entire engagement was classified.
Williams was ordered to keep quiet.
He did — for more than 50 years.

Only after the Cold War ended did the full story come out.
In February of this year, at age 100, he finally received the Medal of Honor.
He is now 101.

One man.
Seven enemy jets.
Four confirmed kills.
And a secret kept for half a century.

Some stories still stop you cold.

President Joe Biden shakes hands with U.S. special operators in Israel on October 18, 2023, in a photo that quickly became one of the biggest OPSEC blunders of the war. The operators, widely identified as members of the Army's SMU, were in Israel in the days after the October 7 Hamas attack, as the U.S. worked to locate Americans held hostage in Gaza.

The photo was taken at an event where Biden met with Israeli first responders. That night, the White House posted it to its official Instagram account without blurring the operators' faces, breaking the long-standing practice of concealing the identities of elite units. The original image showed the faces of several operators, along with a distinctive tattoo on the arm of the man shaking Biden's hand.

The post stayed up for close to an hour before it was deleted. The White House said it removed the photo as soon as the problem was brought to its attention and said it regretted the error. By then, the image had already been widely screenshotted and shared, and the White House faced heavy criticism for exposing the men it was there to thank. It also confirmed what the administration hadn't publicly acknowledged: American special operators were on the ground in Israel.

In this community, protecting identities isn't a formality. It protects operators and their families long after a deployment ends.

A breacher's kit from the Army's SMU in the late 2010s to early 2020s, with Peltor ComTac IV headsets, GPNVG-18 panoramic night vision, and on the rifle, a Wilcox riser with an integrated magnifier mount. The .410 version, to be exact.

The Wilcox riser system was originally designed for a specific customer unit that wanted its optics raised off the receiver for better compatibility with protective masks and other mission gear. The .410 inch version was built to give the lowest rise possible while keeping the EOTech holographic sight and 3x magnifier perfectly aligned. A single motion flips the magnifier out of the way, and a spring-loaded bar lets it come off the rifle completely when it isn't needed.

Up top, the GPNVG-18 gives the operator a 97-degree field of view through four image intensifier tubes, compared to the usual 40-degree "tunnel vision" of a standard set of goggles. Developed by L3 with USSOCOM, it's about as close as night vision gets to seeing the way you do in daylight. Add the ComTac IV for hearing protection and comms, and you have a setup built for the kind of breach where seeing, hearing, and shooting all have to happen at once.

“12,000 FEET UP A FROZEN MOUNTAIN: HE CARRIED HIS PARALYZED TEAMMATE DOWN TO AN IMPROVISED LZ.”

High-altitude mountain rescue leaves zero room for error. When a catastrophic fall in the Colorado backcountry left a Green Beret paralyzed and freezing, Sergeant First Class Bobby Haran stabilized the traumatic injuries, rigged a descent system, and hauled his teammate down a sheer rock face to an area where a rescue chopper could touch its skids.

At the summit of the 14,023-foot Wilson Peak near Telluride, Colorado, SFC Robert "Bobby" Haran an elite mountain instructor with the Special Operations Mountain Warfare Training Center (10th Special Forces Group) watched his teammate’s lead ski strike a submerged rock, releasing the binding and triggering an uncontrolled, 2,000-foot plunge down an icy couloir.

What followed was one of the most remarkable acts of alpine mountaineering and survival in Special Operations history:

Knowing that skiing the steep route solo risked triggering massive avalanches onto his injured partner, Haran descended 2,200 vertical feet on foot across near-vertical ice using only crampons and an ice axe, hauling his teammate's recovered skis to use as an emergency litter.

Reaching his teammate, Haran found him suffering from a fractured sternum, broken hip, shattered shoulder, compound leg fractures, internal bleeding, a torn aorta, and severe hypothermia. Haran stabilized his breathing and wounds in sub-zero winds.

Communicating via emergency satellite with San Miguel County Search and Rescue, Haran rigged a lowering system and moved his paralyzed teammate hundreds of feet further down sheer rock to an improvised alpine landing zone.

After a rescue helicopter hoisted the casualty to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction, Haran skied the remaining backcountry miles solo back to the trailhead.

During a formal ceremony at Fort Carson, Major General Lawrence G. Ferguson presented the Soldier's Medal—the Army's highest peacetime decoration for heroism—to honor Haran's extraordinary valor and skill.

“Bobby, without a doubt, is the only individual that comes to mind that could have performed the way he did that day,” Haran’s NCOIC concluded. “Because of all his training, perseverance, and wherewithal, it resulted in him saving his teammate's life.”

“ONE ROUND. 70 FEET IN THE PITCH DARK. UNDER HEAVY RIFLE FIRE.” — Engaging an active long rifle from behind cover across 23 yards in total darkness using only a standard duty handgun is nearly impossible under live-fire stress. Wounded in the leg by an AR-15 ambush that took the lives of his two partners, Officer Alec Iurato stabilized his breathing, used a patrol cruiser as a shooting platform, and fired the single 9mm shot that ended the gunfight.

“Officer Iurato was confronted with an active, heavily armed shooter who had already killed two police officers and fired more than 80 rounds from an assault rifle. Despite suffering a severe gunshot wound to his leg, Officer Iurato took cover, evaluated the threat, and fired a single precision shot from approximately 70 feet away that neutralized the gunman. His actions were justified, heroic, and saved countless lives.”

 The 70-Foot Shot
The Coordinated Ambush: On October 12, 2022, three officers from the Bristol Police Department responded to a staged 911 call on Redstone Hill Road. As they approached, a gunman concealed in the darkness ambushed them with a semi-automatic AR-15 rifle, firing over 80 rounds of high-velocity ammunition in seconds.

Sergeant Dustin DeMonte and Officer Alex Hamzy were mortally wounded in the initial volley. Both heroes were posthumously promoted to Lieutenant and Sergeant for their ultimate sacrifice protecting the Bristol community.

Officer Iurato sustained a devastating gunshot wound when a rifle round struck his lower leg. Refusing to freeze in the kill zone, he crawled through the dark toward a parked cruiser, placing an engine block and tire between himself and the incoming rounds.

 Body-worn camera audio captures Iurato methodically regulating his respirations while rifle rounds ricocheted off the street. Staging his handgun over the cruiser’s rear quarter panel, he acquired his sights in the darkness, tracked the gunman at roughly 70 feet (23 yards), and broke a single 9mm trigger press directly into the shooter’s head, ending the ambush instantly.

The Fallacy of Handgun Limitations: Standard tactical doctrine often considers handguns effective only within 7 to 15 yards under combat stress. Iurato proved that solid fundamentals—grip, sight picture, and trigger discipline can make a standard service pistol lethal at extended rifle ranges.

Controlling the Stress Inoculation Curve: High-stress gunfights induce intense adrenaline dumps, tunnel vision, and auditory exclusion. Controlling breath tempo under cover resets heart rate just enough to execute precision motor skills.

Exploiting Improvised Hard Cover: Vehicles offer limited ballistic protection from high-velocity rifle fire, but the wheels, axles, and engine block provide substantial cover and a rigid shooting rest for stabilizing long-range pistol fire.

Knowing Roberts was stranded alone surrounded by an entrenched enemy force, Slabinski didn’t wait for a conventional quick-reaction force. He rallied his five remaining teammates, boarded a second Chinook, and ordered the pilots to fly right back into the teeth of the enemy ambush atop the peak.

What unfolded on that ridge defined the unyielding ethos of the Special Operations community:

Stepping off the helicopter into waist-deep snow and freezing blizzards, the team was instantly met by a barrage of interlocking machine-gun and sniper fire from reinforced bunkers just meters away.

 Slabinski led the charge through the snow, repeatedly exposing himself to direct fire and grenade blasts to engage the bunkers, clear enemy fighting positions, and protect wounded teammates.

Trapped on an open, snow-covered precipice and low on ammunition, Slabinski coordinated precision airstrikes within danger-close range of his own position to prevent the enemy from overrunning their line.

14 Hours on the High Ground: Maneuvering his wounded men to a defensible position under relentless fire, Slabinski directed the medical defense and sustained the perimeter for 14 grueling hours until extraction was secured.

On May 24, 2018, President Donald J. Trump presented Master Chief Britt K. Slabinski with the Medal of Honor at the White House, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave a fallen brother behind.

Throwing on a plate carrier over a purple civilian button-up and blue jeans, Craighead breached the complex alone, clearing rooms, neutralizing multiple Al-Shabaab terrorists, and personally escorting hundreds of terrified civilians to safety.

74 years ago today, one American pilot took on seven Soviet MiGs… alone.

Four confirmed kills.
And a secret kept for half a century.

High-altitude mountain rescue leaves zero room for error. When a catastrophic fall in the Colorado backcountry left a Green Beret paralyzed and freezing, Sergeant First Class Bobby Haran stabilized the traumatic injuries, rigged a descent system, and hauled his teammate down a sheer rock face to an area where a rescue chopper could touch its skids.

At the summit of the 14,023-foot Wilson Peak near Telluride, Colorado, SFC Robert "Bobby" Haran an elite mountain instructor with the Special Operations Mountain Warfare Training Center (10th Special Forces Group) watched his teammate’s lead ski strike a submerged rock, releasing the binding and triggering an uncontrolled, 2,000-foot plunge down an icy couloir.

What followed was one of the most remarkable acts of alpine mountaineering and survival in Special Operations history:

Knowing that skiing the steep route solo risked triggering massive avalanches onto his injured partner, Haran descended 2,200 vertical feet on foot across near-vertical ice using only crampons and an ice axe, hauling his teammate's recovered skis to use as an emergency litter.

Reaching his teammate, Haran found him suffering from a fractured sternum, broken hip, shattered shoulder, compound leg fractures, internal bleeding, a torn aorta, and severe hypothermia. Haran stabilized his breathing and wounds in sub-zero winds.

Communicating via emergency satellite with San Miguel County Search and Rescue, Haran rigged a lowering system and moved his paralyzed teammate hundreds of feet further down sheer rock to an improvised alpine landing zone.

After a rescue helicopter hoisted the casualty to St. Mary's Hospital in Grand Junction, Haran skied the remaining backcountry miles solo back to the trailhead.

During a formal ceremony at Fort Carson, Major General Lawrence G. Ferguson presented the Soldier's Medal—the Army's highest peacetime decoration for heroism—to honor Haran's extraordinary valor and skill.

“Bobby, without a doubt, is the only individual that comes to mind that could have performed the way he did that day,” Haran’s NCOIC concluded. “Because of all his training, perseverance, and wherewithal, it resulted in him saving his teammate's life.”

Despite suffering a severe gunshot wound to his leg, Officer Iurato took cover, evaluated the threat, and fired a single precision shot from approximately 70 feet away that neutralized the gunman. His actions were justified, heroic, and saved countless lives.”

 The 70-Foot Shot
The Coordinated Ambush: On October 12, 2022, three officers from the Bristol Police Department responded to a staged 911 call on Redstone Hill Road. As they approached, a gunman concealed in the darkness ambushed them with a semi-automatic AR-15 rifle, firing over 80 rounds of high-velocity ammunition in seconds.

Sergeant Dustin DeMonte and Officer Alex Hamzy were mortally wounded in the initial volley. Both heroes were posthumously promoted to Lieutenant and Sergeant for their ultimate sacrifice protecting the Bristol community.

Officer Iurato sustained a devastating gunshot wound when a rifle round struck his lower leg. Refusing to freeze in the kill zone, he crawled through the dark toward a parked cruiser, placing an engine block and tire between himself and the incoming rounds.

 Body-worn camera audio captures Iurato methodically regulating his respirations while rifle rounds ricocheted off the street. Staging his handgun over the cruiser’s rear quarter panel, he acquired his sights in the darkness, tracked the gunman at roughly 70 feet (23 yards), and broke a single 9mm trigger press directly into the shooter’s head, ending the ambush instantly.

The Fallacy of Handgun Limitations: Standard tactical doctrine often considers handguns effective only within 7 to 15 yards under combat stress. Iurato proved that solid fundamentals—grip, sight picture, and trigger discipline can make a standard service pistol lethal at extended rifle ranges.

Controlling the Stress Inoculation Curve: High-stress gunfights induce intense adrenaline dumps, tunnel vision, and auditory exclusion. Controlling breath tempo under cover resets heart rate just enough to execute precision motor skills.

Exploiting Improvised Hard Cover: Vehicles offer limited ballistic protection from high-velocity rifle fire, but the wheels, axles, and engine block provide substantial cover and a rigid shooting rest for stabilizing long-range pistol fire.

On October 3, 1993, Chief Warrant Officer Mike Durant was flying Super 64 — an MH-60 Black Hawk with the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment — when an RPG hit the tail rotor over Mogadishu.

The crash killed crewmates Bill Cleveland, Ray Frank, and Tommy Field. Badly injured with a broken back and a compound femur fracture, Durant was defended on the ground by Delta Force snipers Gary Gordon and Randy Shughart, who gave their lives holding the site and were posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor.

Held captive for 11 days, Durant was the only American taken alive that day. He returned to flying, retired in 2001 as a CW4 Master Aviator after 22 years of service including Just Cause and Desert Storm, wrote In the Company of Heroes, built Pinnacle Solutions in Huntsville, and later ran in Alabama's 2022 Republican U.S. Senate primary.

33 years later, his story remains a tribute to the Night Stalkers and Delta operators who never made it home. Night Stalkers Don't Quit.

U.S. Army Rangers in Afghanistan around 2018, packing serious heat, including a rare look at the FN Mk 13 EGLM mounted under a SCAR. You don't see this setup often, and that's what makes this photo stand out.

The Mk 13 Mod 0 Enhanced Grenade Launcher Module was developed as part of SOCOM's SCAR program to replace the M203. It fires the full range of NATO standard 40mm low-velocity grenades, uses a double-action trigger that allows multiple strikes on a stubborn primer, and mounts under either the Mk 16 or Mk 17 without adding any length to the rifle. It can also be set up as a stand-alone launcher with its own stock. SOCOM approved it for fielding in 2010.

The Rangers have a long history with the platform. In 2009, the 75th Ranger Regiment became the first SOCOM unit to receive the SCAR, taking delivery of the first 600 rifles. SOCOM later dropped the 5.56mm Mk 16 because it didn't offer enough of an advantage over the M4, which is part of why the EGLM became such an uncommon sight. Most grenadiers ended up running M4s with M203s or M320s instead.

“THEIR HELICOPTER WAS SHOT DOWN: HE LED THE TEAM RIGHT BACK UP THE MOUNTAIN.”

In the early morning hours of March 4, 2002, atop the freezing, 10,000-foot peak of Takur Ghar in eastern Afghanistan, seven American warriors fought one of the most ferocious, desperate close-quarters battles of Operation Anaconda.

Serving as the team leader of a joint reconnaissance element (Mako 30), Senior Chief Petty Officer Britt K. Slabinski and his Navy SEALs were attempting an insertion when their MH-47E Chinook was ambushed by concealed al-Qaeda fighters firing RPGs and heavy machine guns.

During the evasive maneuvers, Petty Officer First Class Neil Roberts was thrown from the rear ramp into the deep snow. The severely damaged helicopter crash-landed miles away in the valley below.

Knowing Roberts was stranded alone surrounded by an entrenched enemy force, Slabinski didn’t wait for a conventional quick-reaction force. He rallied his five remaining teammates, boarded a second Chinook, and ordered the pilots to fly right back into the teeth of the enemy ambush atop the peak.

What unfolded on that ridge defined the unyielding ethos of the Special Operations community:

Stepping off the helicopter into waist-deep snow and freezing blizzards, the team was instantly met by a barrage of interlocking machine-gun and sniper fire from reinforced bunkers just meters away.

 Slabinski led the charge through the snow, repeatedly exposing himself to direct fire and grenade blasts to engage the bunkers, clear enemy fighting positions, and protect wounded teammates.

Trapped on an open, snow-covered precipice and low on ammunition, Slabinski coordinated precision airstrikes within danger-close range of his own position to prevent the enemy from overrunning their line.

14 Hours on the High Ground: Maneuvering his wounded men to a defensible position under relentless fire, Slabinski directed the medical defense and sustained the perimeter for 14 grueling hours until extraction was secured.

On May 24, 2018, President Donald J. Trump presented Master Chief Britt K. Slabinski with the Medal of Honor at the White House, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave a fallen brother behind.

A bond forged in the fires of combat that outlasted the battlefield and saved two lives.

Former DEVGRU (SEAL Team 6) operator Will "Cheese" Chesney seated inside a transport helicopter beside his legendary four-legged teammate, Cairo—the only military working dog on the raid that took down Osama bin Laden.

Pairing up in 2008, Chesney and the Belgian Malinois were virtually inseparable, running hundreds of high-threat direct-action raids across the Global War on Terror. In 2009, Cairo took bullet fire while chasing down enemy insurgents, dragging himself back to Chesney, who fought desperately to keep him alive. Two years later, on the historic night of May 2, 2011, Cairo sat between Chesney’s boots inside a stealth Black Hawk heading into Abbottabad for Operation Neptune Spear—kitted with a Kevlar vest and night vision to secure the perimeter and screen for explosives. In the aftermath of the raid, Cairo was the only operational name released to the public.

The war took a heavy toll on both of them. In 2013, a grenade blast left Chesney with a severe traumatic brain injury and PTSD. As conventional medical treatments failed to break through the crippling migraines and depression, visiting a retired Cairo proved to be his lifeline. Chesney successfully adopted him, allowing the two warriors to nurse each other's scars through Cairo’s final years until cancer claimed the dog in 2015.

Immortalized in Chesney’s memoir No Ordinary Dog, their story stands as the ultimate testament to loyalty between handler and K9.

A man, his dog, and an eternal brotherhood.

“NO ORDERS. NO BACKUP. I POPPED MY TRUNK, GEARED UP, AND WALKED IN ALONE.” — 22 SAS Hero Christian Craighead on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most legendary solo counter-terrorism actions in modern military history, former British 22 Special Air Service (SAS) operator Christian Craighead (known across the world as "Obi-Wan Nairobi") broke down the 2019 DusitD2 hotel siege on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In his own words:

“I was off-duty, sitting in traffic in Nairobi having coffee, when the explosions and automatic gunfire echoed across the city.

I didn’t have a mandate. I didn’t have a squad. I had my personal kit and my rifle stashed in the back of my truck. When I drove toward the smoke and saw people running for their lives, covered in blood, screaming that suicide bombers were inside executing hostages floor by floor, there was no deliberation.

You don’t wait for paperwork while innocent people are being slaughtered.

I pulled my body armor on over my civilian clothes, loaded my rifle, and walked past the police cordon into the gunfire by myself. Every instinct built over decades in the Regiment took over: you find the sound of the shooting, you move toward the danger, and you eliminate the threat before they reach another door.”

Throwing on a plate carrier over a purple civilian button-up and blue jeans, Craighead breached the complex alone, clearing rooms, neutralizing multiple Al-Shabaab terrorists, and personally escorting hundreds of terrified civilians to safety.

For his extraordinary individual valor under fire, Craighead was awarded the Conspicuous Gallantry Cross (CGC) by Queen Elizabeth II.

When terror strikes, most run from the gunfire. Men like Christian Craighead pop the trunk and walk straight toward the sound of the guns.

74 years ago today, one American pilot took on seven Soviet MiGs… alone. 

November 18, 1952.
Navy Lieutenant Royce Williams was flying an F9F Panther off the coast of Korea when he suddenly found himself facing seven Soviet MiG-15s.

Outnumbered.
Outmatched in speed and climb.
And completely alone.

For 35 minutes — the longest dogfight in U.S. Navy history — Williams fought them.
He shot down four of the Soviet jets.
His plane was hit by a 37mm cannon shell, hydraulics failing, yet he still made it back to the carrier and landed.

Because the enemy pilots were Soviet (not North Korean or Chinese), the entire engagement was classified.
Williams was ordered to keep quiet.
He did — for more than 50 years.

Only after the Cold War ended did the full story come out.
In February of this year, at age 100, he finally received the Medal of Honor.
He is now 101.

One man.
Seven enemy jets.
Four confirmed kills.
And a secret kept for half a century.

Some stories still stop you cold.

Matthew Gene "Axe" Axelson (June 25, 1976 – June 28, 2005) was a United States Navy SEAL who was killed in the War in Afghanistan. He was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions and valor during Operation Red Wings, in which he was killed. He served in that operation along with Michael Murphy, Daniel Dietz, and Marcus Luttrell. Dietz and Luttrell were also awarded the Navy Cross, the Purple Heart, and the Navy good conduct medals, where Murphy received the Medal of Honor.

Citation: For extraordinary heroism in actions against the enemy while serving in a four-man Special Reconnaissance element with SEAL Delivery Vehicle Team ONE, Naval Special Warfare Task unit, Afghanistan from 27 to 28 June 2005. Petty Officer Axelson demonstrated extraordinary heroism in the face of grave danger in the vicinity of Asadabad, Konar Province, Afghanistan. Operating in the middle of an enemy-controlled area, in extremely rugged terrain, his Special Reconnaissance element was tasked with locating a high-level Anti-Coalition Militia leader, in support of a follow-on direct action mission to disrupt enemy activity. On 28 June 2005, the element was spotted by Anti-Coalition Militia sympathizers, who immediately revealed their position to the militia fighters. As a result, the element directly encountered the enemy. Demonstrating exceptional resolve and fully understanding the gravity of the situation, Petty Officer Axelson's element bravely engaged the militia, who held both a numerical and positional advantage. The ensuing firefight resulted in numerous enemy personnel killed, with several of the Navy members suffering casualties. Ignoring his injuries and demonstrating exceptional composure, Petty Officer Axelson advised the teammate closest to him to escape while he provided cover fire. With total disregard for his own life and thinking only of his teammate's survival, he continued to attack the enemy, eliminating additional militia fighters, until he was mortally wounded by enemy fire. A champion of freedom, Petty Officer Axelson will be remembered for his self-sacrificing actions in the continuing Global War on Terrorism. By his undaunted courage, fortitude under fire, and unwavering dedication to duty, Petty Officer Axelson reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. He gallantly gave his life for the cause of freedom.

Van Auken and Flannery were traveling together in the lead vehicle on February 14, 2007. They had been tasked with escorting the Kuwait Forensic Team's convoy of 12 vehicles.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time. 

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq. 

When these IEDs exploded, three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles. 

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices. 

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow-on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance. 

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along the west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush. 

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist. 

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience. 

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

The SEALs realized that their odds of survival were slim – but their training and sense of honor told them to take out as many enemies as they could. By the end of a two-hour gunfight that careened through the hills and over cliffs, Murphy, Axelson, and Dietz had fallen.

An estimated 35 Taliban were also dead. Luttrell managed to escape the carnage – badly injured – and slowly crawl away down the side of a cliff.

Dehydrated, with a bullet wound to one leg, shrapnel embedded in both legs, three vertebrae cracked; the situation for Luttrell was grim. Rescue helicopters were sent in, but he was too weak and injured to make contact. Traveling seven miles on foot, he eventually reached a village where he was put under “lokhay warkawal,” Afghan for the protection of the villagers, who fed him and cleaned his wounds. In short order, one of the villagers made his way to a Marine outpost with a note from Luttrell, and U.S. forces launched a massive rescue operation that pulled him from enemy territory. To this day, Luttrell remains indebted to the villagers who risked their lives in his defense. As he told The Washington Post, “In the middle of everything evil, in an evil place, you can find goodness. Goodness. I’d even call it godliness.”

In the early morning hours of March 4, 2002, atop the freezing, 10,000-foot peak of Takur Ghar in eastern Afghanistan, seven American warriors fought one of the most ferocious, desperate close-quarters battles of Operation Anaconda.

Serving as the team leader of a joint reconnaissance element (Mako 30), Senior Chief Petty Officer Britt K. Slabinski and his Navy SEALs were attempting an insertion when their MH-47E Chinook was ambushed by concealed al-Qaeda fighters firing RPGs and heavy machine guns.

During the evasive maneuvers, Petty Officer First Class Neil Roberts was thrown from the rear ramp into the deep snow. The severely damaged helicopter crash-landed miles away in the valley below.

Knowing Roberts was stranded alone surrounded by an entrenched enemy force, Slabinski didn’t wait for a conventional quick-reaction force. He rallied his five remaining teammates, boarded a second Chinook, and ordered the pilots to fly right back into the teeth of the enemy ambush atop the peak.

What unfolded on that ridge defined the unyielding ethos of the Special Operations community:

Stepping off the helicopter into waist-deep snow and freezing blizzards, the team was instantly met by a barrage of interlocking machine-gun and sniper fire from reinforced bunkers just meters away.

 Slabinski led the charge through the snow, repeatedly exposing himself to direct fire and grenade blasts to engage the bunkers, clear enemy fighting positions, and protect wounded teammates.

Trapped on an open, snow-covered precipice and low on ammunition, Slabinski coordinated precision airstrikes within danger-close range of his own position to prevent the enemy from overrunning their line.

14 Hours on the High Ground: Maneuvering his wounded men to a defensible position under relentless fire, Slabinski directed the medical defense and sustained the perimeter for 14 grueling hours until extraction was secured.

On May 24, 2018, President Donald J. Trump presented Master Chief Britt K. Slabinski with the Medal of Honor at the White House, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave a fallen brother behind.

Maj. John Caldwell, of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for his rapid airpower response to an enemy attack on American and allied forces during his deployment to Nuristan province, Afghanistan, May 2, 2011.

The F-16 pilot, then rank of captain, responded to an ambush on a special operations team already taking casualties from effective fire. This timely attack allowed the assault team to momentarily regroup.
Hicks was deployed to the area at that time as well and experienced what it

was like to fly three to five hours a day hovering the war zone just in case of emergency.
"At those moments it seemed quiet, like nothing was going on," said the commander as a description of the sortie Air Force pilots perform covering military members on the ground. "But then in 10 to 20 minutes a decision has to be made resulting in life or death."

Caldwell quickly identified mortar flashes from the mountainside, rapidly derived coordinates and directed his wingman to employ a Joint Direct Attack Munition before refueling. According to the award narrative, he remained as the only kinetic asset protecting the assault force.

"I'd like to say I could take the credit, but it took a combined effort of military services to get the team on the ground out of the valley," said Caldwell.

From his F-16 cockpit, the pilot initiated coordination with the Combined Air Operations Center, conveyed the urgent need for medical evacuation and additional kinetic assets. He also contacted the separated assault team's command element, provided real time updates of the dire situation and gained approval to use any ordnance to protect them. Meanwhile, 90 insurgents began a flanking charge on the friendly position.

"Sadly, there were six American and coalition forces I couldn't help that day; they are the true heroes," said Caldwell. "I was at the right place at the right time and I believe anyone in my squadron would do the same thing."

His award citation said the pilot's life was at risk when he employed an immediate, nonstandard, danger close strafe run into the rugged, midnight black valley, breaking the inexorable charge as the enemy continued to fire with rounds impacting mere inches from the trapped allies. Caldwell immediately re-attacked with an expertly placed, danger close JDAM, completely neutralizing the ambush.

All that said, the pilot still would not call himself "hero."

"You don't get to define yourself as a 'hero,' others do," said Hicks. "Specifically, guys on the ground that night are telling the story of the F-16 that saved them and how they wouldn't be standing today, same goes for their families. The fact you did it speaks volumes on who you are as an aviator and what you did for our country."

The DFC narration said, according to the assault force commander, the presence of Caldwell and his immensely accurate awareness of the situation prevented a catastrophic loss of American lives and directly turned the tide of this engagement.

"Caldwell is not only an awesome fighter pilot, he also exemplifies our core value of 'service before self,'" said Lt. Col. Thomas Seymour, commander of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, where Caldwell has served as weapons flight commander since January. "I think this medal is the result of his skill in the air and his willingness to put himself in harm's way in order to accomplish the mission."

In just a short time stationed here, the commander said the pilot won their group's Flight Commander of the Quarter award and fully embraced his new role as an operational test pilot.

Congress authorized The Distinguished Flying Cross, July 2, 1926, as an award for any military member of the U.S. who exhibited heroism or extraordinary achievement while participating in an aerial fight against an enemy of the U.S.

In most ways, Army Capt. Alex Houston is like any other Army commander. He comes to work every day ready to lead and set the standard for the soldiers who work for him. He diligently performs all of his administrative duties as the 21st Signal Brigade Headquarters and Headquarters Company commander, and he gets down and dirty with the unit during company physical training. He jokes with his staff and even has been known to sing off-key for them.

And he does this all as a wounded warrior. As a platoon leader in Iraq, Houston lost his left hand when his convoy was attacked during a night mission.

The electricity was going on and off while his 1st Cavalry Division unit was on patrol, Houston recalled. “It was so dark -- the kind of dark that you can't even see your hand in front of your face,” he said. As the lights flickered off, the unit's battalion commander came under fire from enemy forces. Although others were in the area, Houston said, he was trained to step up as the ranking officer on the mission, and he headed into the battle to support his commander. He took charge, and while on the radio, he also took a hit.

“There was melted metal all around my hand, and shrapnel went through my arm,” he said, “but I was still on the radio giving information to headquarters.” His duty came before the pain, he said, and his faith in God allowed him to remain calm and accomplish the mission of getting the convoy through the area. “After everyone came over to see how I was, I kept saying, ‘I'm OK.' And I was,” he said. He was rushed to the combat support hospital, and doctors later told him they couldn't save his hand. The division commander presented his Purple Heart while he was still sedated in the combat hospital. “I just said ‘Hooah,'” said Houston, “and they saw the soldier in me.”

Houston spent about a year recovering at Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington, D.C. While there, he had access to many programs that helped wounded warriors transition into the civilian job market. But, when the Army asked him if he wanted to stay in, he said he knew his answer was yes. Houston, who started out as an enlisted soldier, already had made a commitment to a career in the Army. “I made a decision a long time ago that I'm going to give 100 percent,” he said. His injury has not been an impediment at all. According to 21st Signal Brigade Commander Col. Theresa Coles, “He's a true testament to the Warrior Ethos."
